7. Truth and fiction

At my desk and in my head, I've divided a book's actual path to publication into three phases. During the first, strenuous and giddy, it's all words words words, and the writer can hardly keep up with his own output (or at least that's how it feels). Sometimes he can't shut up, and in addition the characters start running all at once, like horses down the last stretch of the Kentucky Derby.

During the second phase, the initial smoothness of the manuscript's momentum gradually thickens into hard labor and more hard labor. I remember the wretched stench of fresh masonry and the rough, splintery boards of the floor at Ughenya on Lagos Island, where Chris finally throws open the cargo hatch after telling Dey say na jet we gotta kill, and a hundred feet below it floats the belly of a fully loaded tanker, the right ship but not the right one. She recognizes it only at the moment when a man in the lifeboat starts telling Keziah about the monstrous cargo lashed to the deck. And you stand there on that humid spring evening, which I know is humid because it hit me that way during the first phase, and you can't see what's wrong but it isn't right, and you go back into your office and say, "Okay, so let's work with this idea for a second," and the editor tells me, "I'm not getting a sense of how she can tell he's lying," and you say "Great, let's think outside the box," and you shrink and deflate and run crawling away from the voices screaming in the headlight.

And now you've come to the third phase, when the editors have recruited three other writers in constricted loadsailing gores at the nautical blind institute, on the Spanish Coast, on Ocean Avenue, doing whatever desperate things they do to blow their nostrils out over troubled (barking, grunting, toiling) seawater, she'll never get this right. Her stride appears so cocky and self-assured, it's like she's a spinster to evoke that spirit I entitled cathedral stage, when engineers and administrators come together to fix the things that froze them up and walked away. The writers have put their noses to your guts and acknowledge your fecal tumult and tried to imagine you as a turtle in the cockpit of plane. Down the west side of Manitou Street, the land opened into a back alley. An old immigrant house sat among other boarded-up houses, stone steps out back and a fence around the garden. Halfway down the alley, Anthony Peralta stood alone on the asphalt with one foot braced against the brick wall. He held a thin strip of folded paper in his fingers, and he stared at it as if he wasn't sure it was really there.

He was five foot eight, curvy across the shoulders, with long hair pulled back in a ponytail and a single silver stud buried on his lower lip. Brown eyes caught the alley light and stayed the color of polished leather, brimming under heavy lids. His jeans rode low, and his black T-shirt clung to a muscled chest that bunched up with his breath. The paper fluttered away from him for a second, then came to rest against his collarbone like a butterfly on a plant leaf.

"Hey, Tony," somebody said.

He must have heard them coming, but he didn't look up. He folded the paper and felt the tight crease in his fingers, and the faint crust of white powder against the knuckles of his right hand.

The somebody turned out to be a little guy named Tony C. Two more people came up behind him, their plans for the night reassembled around the prospect of immediate company. Women in bikinis lay spread-eagled on the apartment roofs above them like satin motel posters. The smell of their wet backs and the heated gravel of the roofs met in the air, clear and cold as perfume.

"Tony, I hear you got some X," Tony C said. "You got one thousand dollars' worth?"

He laughed, the tight-crusted voice of a guy on his second wind. Anthony shook his head at the concrete, at the folded paper in his hand. He had never seen this little Tony before. He pushed the paper into his back pocket.

"I got two," he said.

"Let me see. Let's see," the guy said. "Man, you got the, uh, man, you got the elephant pills. Pink cap, cut 'em clear."

"Three for one-fifty," Anthony said.

In the lineup of cars waiting at the red light on First Avenue North, he listened for horns, tires on curbs, laughter and shouting in other cars, the rattle of deliveries for the businesses a block away. These were sounds that had accompanied him before the pandemic began, and after it returned. He ignored the flutter in his chest and rode through the light, through the city and the daily ritual that took him from his small rented room on Chicago Avenue to his office in the arts center.

    The center was a red brick building set back from the river with space for artists’ studios and loft apartments upstairs. The bike path ended at the loading dock behind the building, and Sidney usually got there at 8:24 AM. Once a week, there was coffee and a cinnamon bun, left outside the door by Gertie Grant. He gave up dialling. Instead he called his brother from the car. "They're going to find out about the money," he said. "We have to get out of here before they do."

His brother said, "You're going to Rat?"

Gil hesitated. Rat was short for Raphael, a messy place in the desert outside of Nogales with a dozen other smuggling families. The Moreaus hadn't kept any ties out there in years. He hadn't even been south of the border since he was a boy.

"You said you'd do it," his brother said. "You promised."

"I know what I promised," Gil said. "But we can get caught. This is retirement money. They're going to look for us for years."

His brother said, "You took it. You have to give it back, or you run."

Gil put the car in gear and turned toward home. His mind was a spinning wheel of terror and hope and exhaustion. Maybe if he just went to sleep and woke up, it would all be over. Maybe, by the time they found out, he and his brother could already be across the border with what was left.

But when he got home he sat down and dialled Rat. They didn't use the phone much, and it took three calls before anyone picked up. A woman he didn't know answered in accented English.

He said, "Is Pete Driscoll there?"

She said, "Who's asking?"

And then he realized that Pete Driscoll had died two years ago. There was nobody left he could trust.

The story of the bridge world right afterward, from the mid-80s to early 2000s, came to me from a series of interviews with several players who, like a couple of characters in the first book, got drawn in to the Gilmore business. Gilmore, Bob, and two other members of the Gilmore partnership, which had bought Bridge University, held out until the very end against efforts by Gil's younger brother Joe to remove them from power. Their story makes up half of the central story in The Last Grandmaster. At the same time, the book follows the careers of several of their students, two of whom, as becomes clear in the second half of the book, have a fateful connection to the Gilmores. Gil felt his knees buckle. He was going to get caught. But then, something surprising happened. One of the trustees who had voted for the audit, Tony Deluca, cleared his throat.

"I..." Tony said, avoiding Gil's eyes. "I may have misspoken. I think Gil's right. We can't just throw around money like that."

Gil felt a surge of relief. Tony owed him a favor. He'd helped him get his son's apprenticeship. One or two more votes and the matter would be dropped.

The second trustee to switch sides looked even more uncomfortable than Tony. She stammered about trusting Gil, about not wanting to spend money unnecessarily. 

By the time Helen Ashby spoke, Gil had convinced himself that he was in the clear. "If that's how you all feel," she said, her voice flat, "so be it."

After the meeting, Gil ran into Helen in the parking lot. She was standing by her car, looking small and tired.

"You had a chance to do the right thing tonight," she said, not looking at him.

"I'm doing the right thing," Gil said. "I'm protecting the fund."

Helen turned to face him. The lines around her eyes looked deeper than he'd ever noticed. 

"You're protecting yourself, Gil," she said. "And you're going to ruin everything we built here because of it."

"You don't understand," he began, but she cut him off.

"Oh, I understand perfectly," she said, and then, without another word, she got into her car and drove away.

Gil stared after her, a chill settling over him that had nothing to do with the evening air. He had saved his skin, but somehow, looking around at the empty parking lot, he felt like he'd lost something much more valuable. He knew he'd now have to find a way to ensure that the auditors never looked beyond the superficial.

The kind of embezzlement Gary Gilmore seems to have committed, by using a phony consulting corporation, is hard for auditors to spot because the money stays in the bank account. But embezzlers often create problems in their paperwork that outsiders can find.

The easiest is to overlook information they try to hide. Missing information is not always inefficient: it may be dishonest. When a bookkeeper prepares a financial statement or list but skips over an account, it means the statement cannot be checked. Be suspicious of blank spaces.

When an accountant, for example, reports that a partner took $74,250 for his share of partnership profits but lists no receipts for a partner's distribution in the same bookkeeping system, the accountant has given a clue that the partner is skimming from the partnership. Someone short of evidence that the distribution was not made may question the partner and an auditor or accountant who has doubts may make further inquiries.

An omission of a significant item, whether in oral, written, or documentary testimony, may be inconsistent with honesty. Accountants who knew the embezzler omitted salary payments in their financial statements. (An accountant's failure to mention salary paid falsely is another sign of dishonesty.)

Another type of dishonesty is inconsistent financial information. Omissions of entries lead to incomplete transactions, which, when viewed beside financial statements that depend on these entries, give conflicting information, or information that does not agree. Such information is likely to be dishonest information.

The auditor should know the embezzler wrote checks to himself and deposited the money in another bank account. When the auditor checked the deposits in the bank account he found they did not agree with what the company had recorded. The auditor had to investigate the differences until he found how much the embezzler had stolen.

Sometimes an embezzler changes financial information. Accountants who knew the embezzler changed the partner's wage allocation among firms listed in a tax return and a financial statement of the partnership.

An embezzler frequently leaves a record of an actual event but altered in some way to conceal dishonesty. Checklists, such as lists of goods that were shipped or received, are particularly liable to alteration. Even the amounts of cash that are received or disbursed must be checked by the auditor against other records.
